title: The Fed Just Raised Rates. What It Means for Your Money
description:
On September 17, 2026, the Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time in more than three years. Here's exactly what that means for your credit card, your mortgage, your car loan and your savings.

Penny the coin explains the Fed's 2026 rate hike with real data: what the Fed actually controls, the rate rollercoaster since 2022, why an oil shock pushed the Fed to act, the split October vote, what happens to credit card rates (now over 21%), mortgages and car loans, why the average savings account still pays almost nothing, a simple rate-hike checklist, and what could happen next.

Data: Fed funds target range (DFEDTARU, DFEDTARL), bank prime loan rate (DPRIME), credit card plan rates (TERMCBCCALLNS) and 48-month new car loan rates (TERMCBAUTO48NS) from the Federal Reserve; 30-year mortgage rate (Freddie Mac, MORTGAGE30US); national savings rate (FDIC, SNDR); CPI and unemployment (BLS); retrieved from FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, through October 2026. October 28 vote: Federal Reserve FOMC statement, October 28, 2026. Deposit insurance: FDIC.

This video is for education only and is not financial advice.
Original script, characters and animation. Narrated with an AI voice.
